beats.beat: Mrs Hale, at the draper's window, sees Rowe and Judith return together at dusk, unchaperoned and laughing, and has the whole parish informed by morning.
Mrs Pike hears it first as triumph, assuming it confirms an attachment, then realizes with horror it is Judith spoken of, and not Louisa.
Flustered, Mrs Pike tells three separate people it was nothing at all, which naturally convinces everyone it was something.
Judith hears an invented version of the story, that she was seen weeping on Rowe's arm, from a girl at the library counter, and goes home changed in temper.
Owen Vane hears it from a customer, closes his shop early, and walks straight to the curate's lodging.

turn.note: Owen sets out to demand Rowe's intentions before he 'comes home,' which is exactly what Chapter 6 opens on.

problems: Opening paragraph shifts into present tense ('The library window looks north up the lane') against the past-tense narration of the rest of the chapter.
'She saw no maid, no Mrs Pike, and no daylight' is a triple negative list that edges toward the banned negative-parallelism pattern even though it is not the exact 'not X, just Y' form.

listenability: Sarah Copp (the gossip's source) and Mrs Copp (the gatehouse maid named in Chapter 3) are close enough in name and unexplained in relation that a listener may conflate them.
trope_note: Serves the chaperone's-absence trope directly through its consequences and shows the meddling matchmaker undone by her own scheme; no fourth trope introduced.
fixes: Correct the tense in the opening paragraph: 'looks north' and 'takes in' should be 'looked north' and 'took in' to match the surrounding past tense.
Clarify whether Sarah Copp is kin to Mrs Copp from Chapter 3, or use a different surname to avoid ear-confusion.

If the chapter needs trimming to hit the target length, the Nye's-cart description in the opening paragraph and the 'Before noon...entirely satisfied' sentence are the most compressible, since both restate the gossip mechanism already dramatized in dialogue.
